paras: The lynching of Bud Spears was the killing of a Black man by a party of masked men who rode up to his house near the Roberts place, twelve miles northwest of Meridian, Mississippi, on Wednesday, December 26, 1888. The attackers acted on a report that Spears was the ringleader of a conspiracy among local Black residents to kill certain white men, a claim the Meridian dispatch traced to an unnamed old man and an overheard conversation. Another Black man at the house was wounded, and in the days that followed white residents arrested Black men as suspected conspirators, seven of whom were acquitted before a justice of the peace. A Times-Democrat special carried the story nationally in January 1889 under headlines that called it a lynching and "Mississippi Race Troubles."

According to the Meridian special, the trouble grew out of the lynching of an unnamed Black man who had entered the house of a Mr. Houston at midnight and tried to murder one of the inmates with an axe. That man was recognized and "afterwards hanged"; the special gave no name, date or place for the hanging, and Black residents had been "making threats" since.
The Brookhaven Leader added that in November a merchant named Cunningham had killed a Black man it described as burglarizing his store, which "aggravated the bad feeling."

Shortly before the Christmas holidays, an old Black man reported that a conspiracy was brewing to kill certain white men in the locality. The special said this report was "corroborated" by an overheard conversation between that man and Spears, who "it was said" was the ringleader, and that "satisfactory evidence" had been produced of Spears's intention to carry out his threat.

On Wednesday, December 26, a party of masked men rode up to Spears's house and "riddled him with buckshot." Another Black man who was at the house was wounded in the hand but escaped. The full dispatch did not state outright that Spears died, but its headlines and the shorter versions, two of which named the attackers "masked white men," treated the shooting as a killing.

White residents of the section then set about "ferreting out the conspirators," arresting Black men and trying them before a justice of the peace. Seven Black men were under arrest on Thursday, January 3, and "upon investigation" were acquitted. As of January 4 a number of men were still under arms, though the special reported that things were "gradually quieting down." No report of an inquest, of any arrest of the masked men, or of a prosecution for the killing appears in the coverage.

Nearly all coverage came from one Meridian special to the New Orleans Times-Democrat, printed in full on January 5 by the Savannah Morning News, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Richmond Dispatch, among others. Editors framed the same text differently: the Savannah paper headed it "Two Negroes Lynched" with the deck "Each One was Eager to Murder White People of the Neighborhood," while the St. Paul Globe ran "Colored Conspirators" over "Southern Regulators Hang One and Riddle Another With Buckshot." The Rock Island Daily Argus headed it "Mississippi Race Troubles," adding that the state was "Very Prolific of Them Just Now."

A one-sentence version, headed "An Assassinator Killed" in the Wichita Eagle, presented Spears as a would-be assassin of the whites who had hanged the axe suspect. Variants ran in weeklies through mid-January: in Michigan and Wisconsin under "A Negro Riddled with Buckshot," with the hangmen softened to whites "accused of hanging" the suspect, and in Kansas under "Masked White Men," datelined "Meridian, Tenn." Only the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian put it bluntly: "Whites murdered" Spears.

The one Mississippi paper found, the Brookhaven Leader, opened its item with "Lauderdale county seems fixing for a race riot" and said that with "Bob Spears" as leader the Black residents "resolved to annihilate the whites"; the item breaks off at "a posse."

The victim's first name appeared as "Bud" in the special, "Bad" in two Northern briefs (likely a misprint) and "Bob" in the Brookhaven Leader. The short wire version dated the Houston axe attack "recently," the Leader "some months since."

framing.detail: Savannah Morning News headline 'Two Negroes Lynched' with deck 'Each One was Eager to Murder White People of the Neighborhood'.
St. Paul Globe: 'Colored Conspirators' over 'Southern Regulators Hang One and Riddle Another With Buckshot'.
Rock Island Argus 'Mississippi Race Troubles ... That State Very Prolific of Them Just Now'; Richmond Dispatch 'Excitement in Mississippi'.
Dakotaian digest: 'Whites murdered a negro named Bad Spears'.
Brookhaven Leader: 'Lauderdale county seems fixing for a race riot'; Black residents 'resolved to annihilate the whites'.
Weekly reprints under 'A Negro Riddled with Buckshot' and 'Masked White Men'.

conflicts.note: 'Bad' is likely a misprint of 'Bud'; 'Bob' is from the only Mississippi paper and cannot be settled from these texts.
